newsitem.title: USA: Tankers cleared of blame for Valdez oil leak.
newsitem.headline: Tankers cleared of blame for Valdez oil leak.

text.p: Tanker operations returned to normal late on Saturday after three vessels docked at the trans-Alaska pipeline's Valdez marine terminal were cleared of blame for a mysterious oil slick found at the port on Friday, officials said.

Most of the floating oil -- which had formed a patchy sheen near the terminal and a half mile (0.8 km) long streak further offshore -- had dissipated or been collected by cleanup crews, Alyeska Pipeline Service Co., the operator of the trans-Alaska pipeline, said.

Examinations by divers and others revealed no cracks or holes in the hulls of the oil tankers, and laboratory tests showed that the discharged oil was not Alaska North Slope crude, the cargo carried by the vessels, Alyeska said.
"It's not crude oil, and it's not any of the products on the vessels," Alyeska spokewoman Jennifer Ruys said.
The U.S. Coast Guard briefly imposed traffic restrictions at the port, limiting vessel arrivals and departures to daylight hours. But later in the day, the Coast Guard lifted the restriction.
By late Saturday, the Arco Fairbanks had left the terminal with its full load of cargo, Ruys said. The Arco Spirit was completing loading and scheduled to depart soon.

The Overseas Ohio, a tanker chartered by British Petroleum, was initially suspected by some officials of leaking the oil because the material was bubbling up next to the ship. But divers found no structural problems with the double-hulled vessel, Alyeska and state officials said.
The Overseas Ohio was scheduled to depart the terminal on Sunday, Ruys said.
Alyeska said it planned further tests to determine whether the spilled oil was linked to the terminal's ballast water source, Ruys said.
About 21 gallons (80 litres) of hydrocarbon product were collected during the cleanup, Alyeska said. No animals or shoreline were affected, the company said.
Oil flow through the trans-Alaska pipeline was undisturbed, despite 36 hours of restrictions on tanker operations, Ruys added.
Alyeska is a consortium owned by seven oil companies with interests on Alaska's North Slope.
British Petroleum, Atlantic Richfield and Exxon are major owners, together holding more than 90 percent of the consortium. Mobil, Unocal, Amerada Hess and Phillips own minor shares.
